title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: Inside the Factory & the Cash Register — Unit Economics & Working Capital

epigraph.quote: Revenue is an engineering achievement; cash flow is a contract-structuring achievement.
epigraph.author: Industrial Credit Desk

web_blocks.html: Marine Electricals runs a direct B2B engineer-to-order and configure-to-order model [2]. It uses no retail dealers; it wins orders via vendor empanelments and tenders with shipyards, colocation firms, and EPCs [2, 4, 11]. Six plants in Goa anchor production, led by the 160,000 sq. ft. Loutulim PTU plant (~800 PTUs/year capacity) [4, 9]. A Vadodara plant, Mumbai/Navi Mumbai engineering offices, and units in the UAE (MEL Power Systems FZC) and Italy (STI S.r.l.) round out the footprint [4, 9, 14].

On supply chain and tech, the firm partners closely with global Tier-1 switchgear OEMs [10]. It is one of the oldest and largest licensed builders of Schneider Electric's BlokSeT line (IEC 61439 and IEC 61641 arc-tested) [10]. It also integrates Siemens parts alongside its own ASTA-certified MEcubE+ panels [10]. Licensing speeds up approvals with hyperscalers that specify global OEMs [10]. Yet it caps gross margin (~29.4% in FY26) because purchased breakers, relays, copper busbars, and transformers dominate costs [15]. Crucially, ICRA's July 2026 credit rationale warns that most of Marine Electricals' contracts are fixed-price in nature, exposing operating margins directly to raw-material and imported-component inflation across 6-to-18-month execution windows if procurement is not locked back-to-back [4].

web_blocks.caption: FY26 Audited Consolidated Unit Economics Waterfall (₹ Crore & Per ₹100 of Revenue)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of ₹877 Cr revenue in FY26, ₹619 Cr (70.6%) went to raw materials, leaving ₹95.00 Cr Operating EBITDA (10.8%) computed from line items (₹94 Cr / 10.7% reported on Screener due to ₹1 Cr integer rounding) and ₹59 Cr PAT (6.7%)—yet working capital absorption turned Operating Cash Flow negative (-₹16 Cr) and Free Cash Flow to -₹43 Cr [1, 15].

web_blocks.html: The FY26 unit-economics waterfall shows the core paradox of this model [1, 15]. On the P&L, scale is helping: staff costs were 8.1% of sales (₹71 crore) and other expenses were 10.5% (₹92 crore) [1, 15]. That lifted operating profit to ₹94 crore reported on Screener (10.7% OPM; ₹95 crore from rounded line items) and net profit to ₹59 crore (6.7% net margin) [1, 15]. At the cash register, every ₹100 of sales required ₹1.82 of operating cash outflow (-₹16 crore CFO) and ₹3.08 of capex (₹27 crore) [1]. The result was negative ₹43 crore of free cash flow [1].

Why does profitable growth consume cash? First, billing and collections follow strict milestones [1]. Shipyards and data-center EPCs hold retention money until site commissioning, keeping Debtor Days at 178 in FY26 (versus 157 in FY25 and 186 in FY23–FY24) and Net Working Capital to Operating Income (NWC/OI) elevated near ~35%, which ICRA expects to persist [1, 4]. Heavy Q4 billing (₹237 Cr in Q4 FY24, ₹251 Cr in Q4 FY25, ₹277 Cr in Q4 FY26) also swells March 31 receivables [1]. Second, executing ₹1,254 crore to ₹3,514 crore of orders demands large Non-Fund Based (NFB) bank guarantees [4, 7]. In July 2026, ICRA noted ₹419.50 crore in rated bank limits across SBI, Yes Bank, IndusInd, and Kotak Mahindra [4]. Short-term Bank Guarantees made up ₹294.50 crore (70%) of that pool, alongside ₹73 crore in Cash Credit [4]. Inventory discipline has actually improved over the past five years [1]. Inventory Days fell from 102 days in FY22 to 50 days in FY26 [1]. Yet Days Payable also tightened from 159 days in FY22 to 135 days in FY26, while Debtor Days stayed elevated at 178 days [1]. That gap kept the Cash Conversion Cycle at 93 days in FY26 [1].

web_blocks.caption: Working Capital & Credit Facility Architecture (FY22–FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: Inventory discipline improved sharply (102 days in FY22 to 50 days in FY26), but 178-day receivables keep the Cash Conversion Cycle near 93 days, causing CFO to swing negative during rapid Q4/H2 ramp-ups [1].

web_blocks.title: Why Bank Guarantees Are the Hidden Bottleneck
paragraphs: In project engineering, NFB bank guarantee limits cap revenue just as much as factory floor space. Without guarantees, a contractor cannot collect advances or bid on ₹50–200 crore data center packages.
ICRA's July 2026 upgrade to [ICRA]A- / [ICRA]A2+ and ₹419.50 crore in rated limits eased this ceiling [4]. Still, interest and guarantee fees (₹19 Cr in FY26, ₹21 Cr TTM) remain a steady drag [1, 4].

book_paragraphs: To understand how Marine Electricals actually makes money—and where that money gets stuck—follow a single 100-rupee note through the FY26 profit-and-loss statement and cash flow statement.

First, note how orders reach the factory. Marine Electricals has no retail dealer network and pays no distributor commissions. It sells directly to pre-qualified B2B buyers—defence shipyards, hyperscale colocation operators, and industrial EPCs—through six plants in Goa, a facility in Vadodara, engineering hubs in Mumbai and Navi Mumbai, and overseas arms in the UAE and Italy. Its newest 160,000 square foot plant in Loutulim, Goa is built to turn out roughly 800 data-center Power Train Units a year.

Now trace 100 rupees of FY26 revenue on 877 crore rupees of consolidated sales. Because Marine Electricals is a system integrator rather than a primary component manufacturer, roughly 70.60 rupees walks out the door immediately to pay for raw materials: circuit breakers, copper busbars, sheet-metal enclosures, relays, and automation hardware. That leaves 29.40 rupees of gross margin—and as ICRA explicitly warned in July 2026, most of the company's contracts are fixed-price, leaving that gross margin exposed to copper, steel, and OEM component inflation whenever delivery stretches over 6 to 18 months. Employee salaries take a lean 8.10 rupees, and factory overheads, testing, and administrative expenses absorb 10.50 rupees. You are left with 10.72 rupees of operating profit.

Below the operating line, depreciation takes 1.71 rupees, interest on working-capital debt and bank-guarantee charges takes 2.17 rupees, other income adds back 1.71 rupees, and taxes take roughly 1.94 rupees. Bottom line: 6.73 rupees of net profit on every 100 rupees of sales, or 59 crore rupees in total.

Now ask the forensic question that separates accounting profit from real cash: how much of that 6.73 rupees actually landed in the bank account in FY26? The answer is minus 1.82 rupees. Operating cash flow was negative 16 crore rupees, and after 27 crore rupees of capital expenditure, free cash flow was negative 43 crore rupees.

That gap is not accounting trickery; it is the structural mechanics of milestone-based project contracting. Notice that factory operations themselves have become markedly leaner: inventory days were cut in half from 102 days in FY22 to 50 days in FY26 as the Goa facilities standardized production. The culprit sits squarely on the receivable line. Debtor Days averaged 178 days in FY26—nearly six months of sales sitting uncollected with shipyards, EPCs, and data center clients, keeping Net Working Capital near 35 percent of operating income, exacerbated by retention money and heavy fourth-quarter billing spikes.

Because institutional customers rarely pay large upfront advances without collateral, Marine Electricals relies heavily on bank guarantees. Out of 419.50 crore rupees of ICRA-rated bank facilities as of July 2026, nearly 294.50 crore rupees—70 percent of the entire banking line—consists of short-term bank guarantees, alongside 73 crore rupees of cash-credit limits spread across SBI, Yes Bank, IndusInd, and Kotak Mahindra Bank. The July 2026 credit upgrade to ICRA A- is a genuine operational win because it opens larger guarantee limits at tighter spreads. Still, until debtor days compress meaningfully below 130 days, rapid revenue growth will continue to act like a sponge on cash.

book_callouts.title: The 178-Day Question
book_callouts.text: When revenue grows 71 percent in a single half-year, a 93-day cash conversion cycle absorbs massive working capital. Watch whether Q3–Q4 collections convert H1 FY27's surge into positive operating cash flow.

book_subsections.title: Following ₹100 Through the Factory and Into Working Capital
paragraphs: How does a rupee of revenue travel through Marine Electricals' income statement and balance sheet? Let's trace the audited FY26 ₹100 waterfall together. Out of every ₹100 of the ₹877 Cr consolidated revenue in FY26, ₹70.58 went straight out the door for raw materials and bought-out components — air circuit breakers, relays, copper busbars, and enclosures sourced largely from Tier-1 OEMs like Schneider Electric and Siemens. That single line tells you the fundamental economics of an integrator: gross margin is capped near ~29.4% because the core switching IP belongs to the global OEM.

From the remaining ₹29.42 of gross profit, employee costs absorbed ₹8.10 and other operating expenses (freight, fabrication, testing, site commissioning) took ₹10.49, leaving ₹10.72 of operating EBITDA. After deducting ₹1.71 for depreciation, ₹2.17 for interest, adding ₹1.71 in other income, and paying ₹1.94 in taxes, accounting net profit came to ₹6.73 per ₹100 of sales (₹59 Cr PAT).

Here is the catch that every serious analyst must watch: that ₹6.73 of accounting profit did not land in the bank account. In FY26, working-capital absorption — driven by 178 debtor days and rising project receivables — turned operating cash flow negative at -₹1.82 per ₹100 of revenue (-₹16 Cr CFO). Add -₹3.08 per ₹100 in capital expenditure (-₹27 Cr capex), and free cash flow was -₹4.90 per ₹100 (-₹43 Cr FCF). Until collections accelerate below 120 debtor days, rapid top-line growth will continue to consume cash.

book_subsections.title: Customer Qualification, Bank Guarantees & The Non-Fund-Based Bottleneck
paragraphs: If you want to understand why electrical integrators live or die by their credit lines, look at ICRA's July 2026 rating action upgrading Marine Electricals' ₹419.50 Cr bank facilities to [ICRA]A- and [ICRA]A2+. In B2B power distribution and naval defence, a company cannot simply ship a switchboard and collect cash on delivery. Customers like Mazagon Dock, Garden Reach Shipbuilders, Princeton Digital Group, and STT GDC require advance bank guarantees, performance bank guarantees, and retention money held back until site commissioning and defect-liability periods conclude.

Those non-fund-based (NFB) bank limits act as the oxygen supply for a ₹3,514 Cr order book. When debtor days stretch to 178 days — as they did in FY26 — cash gets locked inside receivables and unbilled contract assets (pushing Other Assets to ₹953 Cr by September 2026). As long as banks and rating agencies stay comfortable, the wheel keeps spinning. If customer payments slip even by 30 to 45 days during a broader capex slowdown, NFB utilization tightens rapidly, squeezing both execution speed and equity returns.

book_subsections.title: Why Integration Speed Beats Pure Price in Data-Center Tenders
paragraphs: When a hyperscale developer like Princeton Digital Group or CtrlS commissions a 30 MW data hall in Navi Mumbai or Chennai, every month of construction delay costs millions in lost colocation lease revenue. That time-value-of-money dynamic explains why containerized Power Train Units built in Goa have gained rapid adoption: pre-wiring switchgear, busducts, and protection relays inside a weatherproof steel enclosure shifts months of chaotic on-site electrical work into a controlled factory assembly line.

However, fast factory delivery does not automatically translate into fast cash collection. Because data-center projects involve multi-stage site acceptance testing, third-party MEP sign-offs, and milestone retention clauses, Marine Electricals still carries 178 Debtor Days — requiring disciplined credit control to prevent backlog growth from starving working capital.
